title: Market Participants in the Securities Market
big_picture: Think of the securities market as a busy railway system. Investors are the passengers with money, issuers are the destinations that need it, intermediaries (exchanges, clearing corporations, depositories, brokers, custodians) run the trains and stations, and SEBI is the railway authority that writes the rule book and punishes those who break it. This chapter is a who's who of that system plus the main laws (SCRA, SEBI Act, Depositories Act, Companies Act, PMLA, insider trading and PFUTP rules) that keep it honest.
exam_focus: Investor categories: RII (₹2 lakh), institutional, NII, FPI Category I vs II, accredited investor thresholds and validity
Membership types (only trading, self-clearing, trading-cum-clearing, PCM) and who has trading vs clearing rights
Clearing corporation basics: novation, pay-in / pay-out; depositories NSDL and CDSL and who can be a DP
Broker eligibility: age 21, HSC, 2 years' experience, ₹30 lakh paid-up capital; fit and proper; Authorised Persons
Who regulates what: SEBI, RBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, IFSCA; rules vs regulations; Section 24 of the Companies Act
PMLA: offence, 3-7 years punishment, 5-year record keeping, burden of proof on the accused
Insider trading (connected person, 6 months, UPSI list) vs PFUTP / front running vs dabba trading penalties

sections.title: Introduction: Who Is in the Market

blocks.text: Savers (surplus generators) and spenders (deficit generators) meet in the securities market. Investors place surplus funds in securities issued by issuers, in return for interest, dividend, capital appreciation, bonus and so on. Intermediaries are the conduits between them, and regulators supervise the whole process.

Regulators develop fair market practices, regulate issuers, investors and intermediaries, protect investors, and ensure high service standards from intermediaries, a supply of quality securities and non-manipulated demand.
Four I's and an R: Investors, Issuers, Intermediaries, and the Regulator watching all three.
Based on primary issue categories, investors are Retail Individual Investors (RII), Institutional Investors and Non-Institutional Investors (NII).

head: Category
Who
Note
rows: Applies / bids for not more than ₹2 lakh
Domestic financial institutions, banks, insurance companies, mutual funds, Foreign Portfolio Investors, others specified by SEBI
FPI = entity established or incorporated outside India that invests in India
Anyone other than RII and institutional: family offices, corporates, partnership firms etc.
So an individual bidding ₹3 lakh in an IPO falls here, not in RII

blocks.text: The SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019 split FPIs into two categories:

items.title: Category I
points: Government and government-related investors: central banks, sovereign wealth funds, international / multilateral organisations
Entities controlled or at least 75% owned (directly / indirectly) by them
Pension funds and university funds
Appropriately regulated entities: insurers, banks, AMCs, investment managers / advisers, portfolio managers, broker / swap dealers
Entities from FATF member countries (with conditions)
Entities managed by a FATF-country Category I FPI manager, or 75%+ owned by an eligible FATF-country entity

items.title: Category II
points: Appropriately regulated funds not eligible for Category I
Endowments and foundations; charitable organisations
Corporate bodies; family offices; individuals
Regulated entities investing on behalf of their clients
Unregulated funds in the form of limited partnerships and trusts
Note: Category II corporate bodies, individuals and family offices are treated as non-institutional

blocks.text: Category I = governments, regulated institutions and FATF-linked big players. Category II = everyone else.

Accredited Investors (AIs) are investors who understand financial products and their risk-return and can take informed decisions (called Qualified or Professional Investors elsewhere). SEBI has introduced the concept in India.

head: Who
Eligibility
rows: Individuals, HUFs, family trusts, sole proprietorships
Annual income ≥ ₹2 crore; OR net worth ≥ ₹7.5 crore (≥ ₹3.75 crore in financial assets); OR income ≥ ₹1 crore + net worth ≥ ₹5 crore (≥ ₹2.5 crore in financial assets)
Each partner independently meets the individual criteria
Rupee equivalent of their income / net worth
Central and State Governments, their developmental agencies and funds, QIBs under ICDR 2018, Category I FPIs, sovereign wealth funds, multilateral agencies, others SEBI specifies

blocks.text: Individual AI test is 2, or 7.5, or 1 + 5 (crore). The financial-asset part is always half the net worth figure (3.75 of 7.5, 2.5 of 5). Trusts and companies: a flat ₹50 crore.

items: Accreditation Agencies: subsidiaries of depositories and stock exchanges (or other institutions meeting SEBI criteria) issue the certificate, solely on the basis of KYC and financial information.

Validity: criteria met for the preceding 1 financial year = valid 2 years; met in each of the preceding 2 financial years = 3 years; newly incorporated entity meeting the net worth test on the application date = 2 years.

Benefits: lower ticket size than the regulatory minimum; a 'regulation-light' framework (relaxed prudential norms, filings, audit / valuation / reporting frequency); access to products offered exclusively to AIs.

blocks.text: Market makers provide liquidity by giving two-way (buy and sell) quotes continuously, for a minimum amount and with a reasonable bid-ask spread. They work under SEBI or exchange guidelines (SEBI market maker circular of January 20, 2000; 'Liquidity Enhancement Scheme in the Equity Cash and Equity Derivatives Segments', April 23, 2014). In regular cash and derivatives markets, liquidity schemes are mainly run by exchanges, but on the SME exchange, market making is mandatory for all listed and traded scrips.
RII limit is ₹2 lakh (not ₹5 lakh or ₹10 lakh). AI certificate valid for 2 years (1 year of data) or 3 years (2 years of data). Market making is compulsory only on the SME exchange.

Public and private sector companies, banks and FIs tap the market to fund expansion; even mutual funds mobilise savings. Domestically, issuers raise money through equity shares, preference shares, debentures and bonds, by public offer and / or private placement. Since the 1991 reforms, Indian companies can also raise equity abroad.

head: Instrument
What it is
rows: Negotiable instrument issued by a foreign depository bank other than in the US, representing shares of a foreign company; generally traded on European exchanges
Negotiable certificate issued by a US depository bank; trades on US markets like a domestic share
Bond issued by an Indian company to non-residents in foreign currency; fixed coupon; convertible into shares at a predetermined price
Commercial loans (bank loans, buyers' / suppliers' credit, securitised instruments, FRNs, fixed rate bonds) from recognised foreign sources; popular because borrowing costs abroad are low
Rupee-denominated bond issued outside India by an Indian entity
Certain Indian companies may now list directly on overseas exchanges
blocks.caption: Raising money abroad: regulated mainly by RBI under FEMA, and by SEBI for equity instruments

items.title: ADR / GDR
points: Indian company raises money abroad
Listed overseas (US / Europe)

items.title: IDR
points: Foreign company raises money in India, in rupees
Listed in India; Standard Chartered Bank was the first IDR issuer

blocks.text: ADR = America; GDR = the rest of the Globe (mainly Europe). Masala = Indian flavour (rupee) served abroad.

head: Regulation
What it covers
rows: SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018 (ICDR)

Conditions and eligibility for public and rights issues; obligations of issuers and intermediaries; preferential issues, QIPs, bonus issues; IDRs; disclosures. The merchant banker / lead manager manages the issue and acts as Book Running Lead Manager (BRLM) in book-built issues
SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (LODR)
Listing agreement with the exchange; disclosures and obligations of listed entities; in-principle approval before further issues
Securitised Debt Instruments and Security Receipts Regulations, 2008; Municipal Debt Securities Regulations, 2015; Non-Convertible Securities Regulations, 2021

head: Where the company is listed
In-principle approval needed from
rows: On exchange(s) with nationwide trading terminals
The nationwide exchange(s) where it is listed
All exchanges where the securities are proposed to be listed
On both nationwide and non-nationwide exchanges
blocks.caption: LODR: in-principle approval before issuing further shares

blocks.text: Intermediation means enabling buyers and sellers (through information and facilitation) to trade securities and acquire all rights attached to them. Stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories are together called Market Infrastructure Institutions (MIIs).

head: MII
Core job
Key law
rows: Trading platform where buyers and sellers meet
Clearing, settlement and risk management; central counterparty
Holds securities electronically; transfers by book entry

blocks.text: Stock exchange: trading moved from the 'ring' to online systems (VSATs, leased lines, internet). SCRA defines it as a body of individuals constituted before corporatisation and demutualisation (sections 4A, 4B), or a body corporate under the Companies Act, for assisting, regulating or coordinating dealing in securities. Its functions:

items: Provide the trading platform
Disseminate information
Investor education, awareness and protection
Facilitate grievance redressal
Surveillance and investigation
Listing of securities and monitoring compliance of listed companies
Inspection and monitoring of member compliance

blocks.text: An exchange is seven things at once: a market, a newsroom, a school, a complaints desk, a police station, a gatekeeper (listing) and an inspector (of members).

Clearing corporation: under the SECC Regulations, 2018, an entity that clears and settles trades in securities dealt on a recognised exchange; includes a clearing house and a limited purpose clearing corporation (Chapter IV-A of SECC). Its functions: clearing, settlement and risk management. It acts as central counterparty, giving a financial guarantee for all trades: this is called novation.

items.title: Pay-in (first phase)
points: Clearing members and custodians (for institutional deals) bring money and / or securities into the clearing corporation

items.title: Pay-out (second phase)
points: The clearing corporation pays money / delivers securities out to clearing members and custodians

blocks.text: Ravi sells 100 shares at ₹1,500 and Meena buys them; they never know each other. After the trade, the clearing corporation becomes the buyer to Ravi and the seller to Meena. If Meena defaults, Ravi still receives ₹1,50,000 from the clearing corporation. That guarantee is novation.
blocks.title: Novation

blocks.text: Depository: holds securities in electronic form and transfers them by book entry, enabling paperless trading with speed, accuracy and safety. Under the Depositories Act, 1996 it is a company formed under the Companies Act, 1956 and registered under section 12(1A) of the SEBI Act, 1992. India has two: NSDL and CDSL.

items: Depositories serve clients through agents called Depository Participants (DPs), appointed by the depository with SEBI approval.
Who can be a DP: banks, FIs, NBFCs, clearing corporations, RTAs, custodians, State Financial Corporations and SEBI-registered trading members.
Besides custody and dematerialisation, depositories offer transaction services (buying, selling, transfer).

sections.title: Trading Members, Clearing Members and Authorised Persons

blocks.text: A stock broker is a person with trading rights on a recognised exchange, including a trading member. He can trade on his own account and for clients, and may be an individual (sole proprietor), partnership firm, LLP, company or bank (banks may become members of the currency derivatives segment subject to prudential norms). Investors cannot access the exchange directly; they must trade through a registered broker. Clearing members have clearing and settlement rights in a recognised clearing corporation.

head: Membership type
Trading rights
Clearing rights
Clears whose trades
rows: None: must clear through a trading-cum-clearing member or a PCM
Only its own trades (own account and its clients), not custodial participants
Own trades plus other trading members and custodial participants

blocks.text: PCM eligibility: SEBI-registered custodians and banks recognised by the clearing corporation. Custodians too are clearing members but not trading members: they settle trades of a broker's clients when assigned and must confirm whether they will settle.
PCM = Pure Clearing Member: it never trades. 'Only trading member' is the opposite: trades but never clears.
Registration: under the SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 2026 (which replaced the 1992 Regulations), a new entity applies to SEBI through the stock exchange or clearing corporation.

items: One certificate of registration from SEBI, whatever the number of exchanges, clearing corporations or segments; operating on each exchange / segment still needs that exchange's approval.
No separate registration is needed for a broker to act as clearing member (with the clearing corporation's approval), or vice versa.
SEBI sets segment-wise net worth and deposits, and fees; membership of each segment is separate.
Admission criteria: age, capital adequacy, financial track record, education, experience and 'fit and proper' status (SEBI Intermediaries Regulations, 2008); exchanges may add more.

blocks.text: Base Minimum Capital (BMC): a deposit with the exchange against which no trading exposure is allowed, set by the member's risk profile (detailed in Chapter 4).

head: Criteria
Individual
Partnership firm / LLP
Company
rows: At least 2 years as partner, authorised assistant, authorised remisier or apprentice to a member
Identify Dominant Promoter Group (DPG); changes need prior Exchange / SEBI permission
Minimum paid-up equity ₹30 lakh (currently); DPG norms
blocks.caption: Membership eligibility (Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957)

blocks.text: 21 - 2 - HSC - 2: age 21, two designated persons, HSC, two years of experience. Add ₹30 lakh paid-up capital for companies.

items: LLP / company: designated partners or directors must not be disqualified under rule 8 of SCRR, nor have been directors / partners of a member declared defaulter or expelled.
SEBI also checks infrastructure, directors' experience and disciplinary proceedings against key management persons.

At all times the proprietor, one designated director / partner, or the Compliance Officer must hold the SEBI / exchange certification (a continued admittance norm), and net worth and deposits must be maintained.

blocks.text: Fit and proper person (Schedule II, SEBI Intermediaries Regulations, 2008): for the applicant, broker, AP, trading or clearing member, and its principal officer, directors, promoters and key management persons, SEBI may consider:

items: Integrity, reputation and character
Absence of convictions and restraint orders
Competence, including financial solvency and net worth
Absence of categorisation as a wilful defaulter

blocks.text: Fit and proper = I-C-C-W: Integrity, no Convictions, Competence, not a Wilful defaulter.

Authorised Person (AP): not an exchange member, but any person (individual, partnership firm, LLP or body corporate) appointed by a stock broker to provide access to the exchange's trading platform as the broker's agent.

items: Appointed with exchange approval: specific prior approval for each AP, and it is segment specific.
Must meet SEBI / exchange criteria and have adequate office space, equipment and manpower.
Written agreement in the exchange-prescribed form: scope, responsibilities, confidentiality, commission sharing, termination.
The broker is responsible for all acts of omission and commission of its AP, as if they were its own.

blocks.text: One SEBI registration covers all exchanges and segments, but exchange approval and segment membership are still separate. An AP is not a member of the exchange.
A custodian carries on the business of providing custodial services and must be registered with SEBI. Its job is to safeguard clients' securities and track corporate actions for them.

items: Maintain the client's securities account
Collect benefits or rights accruing on the securities
Keep the client informed of issuer actions affecting those benefits or rights
Maintain and reconcile records of these services

blocks.text: Custodians are clearing members, not trading members. When a trade is assigned to them they must confirm whether they will settle it. If the custodian fails to confirm, the obligation falls on the trading member (or its clearing member) that executed the trade.

A foreign fund buys ₹50 crore of shares through broker XYZ and assigns the trade to its custodian. If the custodian confirms, it settles the trade. If it does not confirm, XYZ (or XYZ's clearing member) must settle the ₹50 crore.
blocks.title: Custodian confirmation

blocks.text: Regulators make sure participants behave so that the market stays a trusted source of finance and investors are protected.

head: Regulator
Regulates
rows: Securities market and the commodity derivatives market
Unified regulator for financial products, services and institutions in the IFSC
Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Corporate Affairs

items: Most powers under SCRA are exercised by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA), Ministry of Finance; a few by SEBI. SEBI also exercises DEA's SCRA powers concurrently.
RBI concurrently exercises powers over contracts in gold-related securities, money market securities, securities derived from these, and ready forward contracts in debt securities.
The SEBI Act and the Depositories Act are administered primarily by SEBI.
Rules under securities laws are framed by the Government; regulations are framed by SEBI; SEBI administers all of them.
Companies Act powers on issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend are administered by SEBI for listed public companies and those proposing to list.
Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) enforce their own rules and the securities laws relevant to them.

blocks.text: Government writes Rules, SEBI writes Regulations.
SEBI was established under Section 3 of the SEBI Act, 1992, an Act of Parliament. Its primary role: protect investors' interests, promote development of the securities market, and regulate it.

items: Protecting the interests of investors in securities
Promoting the development of the securities market
Regulating business in stock exchanges and other securities markets
Registering and regulating stock brokers, Authorised Persons etc.
Promoting and regulating self-regulatory organisations
Prohibiting fraudulent and unfair trade practices
Calling for information, inspections, inquiries and audits of exchanges, intermediaries, SROs, mutual funds and others

blocks.text: SEBI's three-word mission: Protect, Promote, Regulate.

sections.title: Regulatory Framework: The Four Acts and Key Rules

blocks.text: Liberalisation of the Indian securities market began in 1992, aiming to protect investors, regulate and develop the market.

head: Act
Core purpose
rows: Gives SEBI statutory powers to protect investors, develop and regulate the market
Central Government control over exchanges, contracts in securities and listing
Allows multiple depositories; led to NSDL and CDSL
Issue, allotment, transfer of securities and company management; delegates securities powers to SEBI
blocks.caption: The four main Acts

blocks.text: In date order: SCRA 56, SEBI 92, Depositories 96, Companies 2013.

head: Other key law / regulation
Year
rows: SC(R) (Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations) Regulations
SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to the Securities Market) Regulations
SEBI (Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations

blocks.text: SEBI Act, 1992: jurisdiction over companies that list or propose to list (issue of capital and transfer of securities) and over all intermediaries and persons associated with the securities market. SEBI can conduct enquiries, audits and inspections, adjudicate offences, register and regulate intermediaries and penalise violations. It has full autonomy. Its orders are appealable before the Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT).

SCRA, 1956: direct and indirect control of virtually all aspects of securities trading and exchanges, to prevent undesirable transactions. It gives the Central Government jurisdiction over (a) stock exchanges, through recognition and continued supervision, (b) contracts in securities and (c) listing. Exchanges frame their own listing regulations, which must conform to the minimum listing criteria in the Rules.

Depositories Act, 1996: allows multiple depositories to create competition. Only a company under the Companies Act, sponsored by specified institutions, can set up a depository, after getting a certificate of registration and a certificate of commencement of business from SEBI. A depository cannot open accounts directly; investors deal through its DPs. The Act sets out the rights and obligations of depositories, DPs, issuers and beneficial owners.

Companies Act, 2013: covers issue, allotment and transfer of securities, disclosure standards in public issues, underwriting, premium and discounts, rights and bonus issues, interest and dividends, and annual reports. Section 24 delegates power to SEBI: provisions on (i) issue and transfer of securities and (ii) non-payment of dividend, for listed companies and those intending to list, are administered by SEBI; in any other case, by the Central Government.
The only highlighted change in this chapter is in the sample question on this point: 'Stock Exchanges' now appears as option (d). The answer is still SEBI.

SCRR, 1957: made by the Central Government under section 30 of SCRA. Covers application for and recognition of exchanges, qualifications for membership, books and documents exchanges and brokers must maintain, and listing requirements (including units of Collective Investment Schemes).

SECC Regulations, 2018 (notified October 3, 2018): recognition, net worth, ownership and governance of exchanges and clearing corporations; monitoring of shareholding limits and 'fit and proper' criteria for all shareholders; KMP compensation as per SEBI norms; listing of exchanges; and segregation of regulatory departments from other departments. Read with SCRA and SCRR.
The SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 2026 replaced the 1992 Regulations. They cover registration of stock brokers and clearing members and their operational and general obligations.

Chapter VIII contains the code of conduct (full list in Annexure 1). Among other things the broker must maintain high standards of integrity, promptitude and fairness; act with due skill, care and diligence; avoid manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive transactions and rumours; and never create a false market.

items: Execute client orders faithfully at the best available market price.
Issue a contract note for all transactions without delay, in the form specified by the exchange.
Maintain prescribed books of account, records and documents (Chapter 3).

blocks.text: An option reading 'SEBI (Stock Brokers) Regulations, 1992' is outdated: the current framework is the 2026 Regulations.

sections.title: Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and SEBI AML Guidelines

blocks.text: PMLA defines money laundering as any process or activity connected with proceeds of crime, including its concealment, possession, acquisition or use, and projecting or claiming it as untainted property. The Act aims to prevent money laundering and confiscate property derived from or involved in it.

Section 3 (offence): anyone who directly or indirectly attempts, knowingly assists, is knowingly a party to, or is actually involved in any of six activities with proceeds of crime: concealment, possession, acquisition, use, projecting as untainted, claiming as untainted. It is a continuing activity as long as the person enjoys the proceeds.

head: Section
What it says
rows: Punishment: rigorous imprisonment of 3 to 7 years plus fine; up to 10 years if the proceeds relate to offences in paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule (the narcotics offences)
On confiscation, property vests absolutely in the Central Government, free of encumbrances

Adjudicating Authority has civil court powers (Code of Civil Procedure): discovery and inspection, enforcing attendance and examination on oath, compelling production of records, evidence on affidavits, issuing commissions. Summoned persons must attend and tell the truth; proceedings are judicial proceedings under IPC sections 193 and 228
Enhanced due diligence for specified transactions
Powers of authorities for summons, searches and seizures
Burden of proof on the accused: proceeds are presumed involved in money laundering unless proved otherwise
Appellate Tribunal and appeals to it
Appeals to the High Court against Appellate Tribunal orders, within the stipulated time
Central Government designates Courts of Session as Special Courts

blocks.text: Section 12: every reporting entity (banking company, financial institution, intermediary, or person carrying on a designated business or profession) must:

items: (a) Keep records of all transactions so that each can be reconstructed: 5 years from the date of the transaction.
(b) Furnish information on prescribed transactions, attempted or executed, to the Director (Director / Additional / Joint Director appointed under section 49).
(c) Keep identity records of clients and beneficial owners, account files and correspondence: 5 years after the business relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later.
(d) Keep all such information confidential. The Central Government may exempt any reporting entity or class.

blocks.text: Section 12AA, enhanced due diligence (EDD): before each specified transaction the reporting entity must (a) verify the client's identity by Aadhaar authentication (or another prescribed mode if the person cannot get Aadhaar), (b) examine ownership and financial position, including source of funds, and (c) record the purpose of the transaction and the intended relationship. EDD information is kept 5 years from the transaction date. If the client does not comply, the transaction is not allowed. If it looks suspicious, monitoring of the client is stepped up.

items: Specified transactions: cash withdrawal or deposit above a prescribed amount; foreign exchange transactions above a prescribed amount; high value imports or remittances; others prescribed in the interest of revenue or for high money-laundering / terror-financing risk.

blocks.text: PMLA in numbers: 3 to 7 years in jail (10 for narcotics-linked proceeds), records for 5 years. Six verbs of the offence: hide, hold, get, use, pass off, claim (as clean).
Transaction records: 5 years from the transaction. Identity records: 5 years from the end of the relationship / account closure, whichever is later. Both are 5, never 7, 8 or 10.

SEBI AML / CFT master circular: explains PMLA in practice and the steps to discourage and detect money laundering and terror financing. It covers all section 12 SEBI Act intermediaries (stock brokers, share transfer agents, bankers and registrars to an issue, trustees to a trust deed, AMCs, DPs, merchant bankers, portfolio managers, investment advisers), stock exchanges and depositories: all reporting entities under PMLA and the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005. The Rules let SEBI specify the records to keep and require an internal mechanism to detect and report transactions.

items: Topics: AML policies and written procedures, client due diligence, acceptance and identification, reliance on third parties, risk management, suspicious transaction monitoring and reporting, freezing of funds, records, reporting to FIU-India, designated officers, hiring, training and investor education.

Clients are classified Low, Medium or High risk using location, nature of business, volume and value of turnover, nature of transactions and manner of payment. Special category clients (e.g. politically exposed persons, clients from high-risk countries) may get an even higher risk rating.
Intermediaries must appoint a Principal Officer and a Designated Director for PMLA compliance.

blocks.text: Insider trading is dealing in a company's securities on the basis of unpublished price sensitive information (UPSI) to make a profit or avoid a loss. It gives insiders an unfair edge and damages market integrity, so it is an offence under the SEBI (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015, in force from May 2015. They define insiders, restrict communication and trading, require disclosures, and set systems for listed and to-be-listed companies and intermediaries.

Insider (Reg 2(g)) = (i) a connected person, or (ii) anyone in possession of or having access to UPSI, however obtained. The onus of showing possession / access is first on the person levelling the charge; the trader may then show he had no possession or access, did not trade, or is covered by an exonerating circumstance.

Connected person (Reg 2(d)): anyone who is, or during the 6 months before the act was, associated with the company in any capacity (frequent communication with officers, contractual, fiduciary or employment relationship, director, officer, employee, professional or business relationship) that gives or may reasonably give access to UPSI.

head: Deemed connected persons (unless the contrary is established)
rows: Relatives of connected persons; persons sharing household or residence with them
Intermediaries under section 12 of the SEBI Act, and their employees / directors
Investment companies, trustee companies, AMCs, and their employees / directors; members of a mutual fund's board of trustees or its board
Officials of a stock exchange, clearing house or clearing corporation; officials / employees of a SEBI-recognised SRO
Board members or employees of a public financial institution (Section 2(72), Companies Act, 2013)
Any concern, firm, HUF, company or AOP in which a director, his immediate relative or the company's banker holds more than 10%
A firm, its partner or employee where a connected person is also a partner

blocks.text: UPSI (Reg 2(n)): information about a company or its securities, not generally available, that is likely to materially affect the price once public. Ordinarily includes:

items: Financial results; dividends; change in capital structure
Mergers, de-mergers, acquisitions, delisting, disposals, expansion, award or termination of orders / contracts outside the normal course
Changes in key managerial personnel (other than superannuation or end of term), and resignation of a Statutory or Secretarial Auditor
Change in ratings, other than ESG ratings
Proposed fund raising; agreements that may affect management or control
Initiation of a forensic audit and receipt of the final forensic audit report
Outcome of litigation or disputes that may affect the company
Grant, withdrawal, surrender, cancellation or suspension of key licences or regulatory approvals

blocks.text: Structure: Chapter II restrictions on communication and trading by insiders; Chapter II(A) the same for mutual fund units; Chapter III disclosures of trading by insiders. The UPSI list is illustrative, not exhaustive.

Not UPSI: a KMP retiring on superannuation or end of term, and an ESG rating change. UPSI: an auditor's resignation, any other rating change. Connected-person look-back is 6 months; the holding threshold is more than 10%.
The SEBI (Prohibition of Fraudulent and Unfair Trade Practices relating to the Securities Market) Regulations, 2003 let SEBI investigate market manipulation and fraudulent or unfair practices.

Fraud (Reg 2(1)(c)): any act, expression, omission or concealment, deceitful or not, by a person or his agent or accomplice, to induce another to deal in securities, whether or not there is wrongful gain or avoided loss. Includes knowing misrepresentation or concealment, active concealment, promises with no intent to perform, reckless or baseless statements, deception that denies informed consent, acts other laws call fraudulent, and an issuer's misinformation that moves the market price.

items: Regulation 3: no person shall, directly or indirectly, (a) deal in securities fraudulently; (b) use a manipulative or deceptive device in connection with listed / to-be-listed securities; (c) employ any device, scheme or artifice to defraud; (d) engage in any act or practice that operates as fraud or deceit.

Regulation 4(1): no manipulative, fraudulent or unfair trade practice. Always deemed included: diversion or siphoning of a listed company's assets or manipulating its books to influence the price, and trading through mule accounts.

head: Theme
Deemed manipulative, fraudulent or unfair (Reg 4(2))
rows: Creating a false or misleading appearance of trading; deals not meant to transfer beneficial ownership but to move prices; transactions without intention to perform or to change ownership; circular trades between persons including intermediaries
Inducing others (even by paying them) to trade to move prices; manipulating a price, incl. a reference / benchmark price
Inducing subscriptions (e.g. by advancing money) to fraudulently secure minimum subscription; illegal mobilisation of funds through a collective investment scheme
Publishing untrue information (results, M&A, approvals) while dealing; spreading false or misleading information or advice through any media, physical or digital; planting false news

Trading for a client without knowledge or instructions; misusing client funds / securities held in a fiduciary capacity; inducing trades to boost brokerage; predating or falsifying contract notes, client instructions or statements; mis-selling
Placing an order while holding non-public information about a substantial impending transaction in that security, its underlying or derivative

Selling, dealing or pledging stolen, counterfeit or fraudulently issued securities (physical or demat), unless the person was a holder in due course or the securities were earlier traded in a bona fide transaction

blocks.text: Mis-selling: selling securities or related services by knowingly making false or misleading statements, knowingly concealing material facts or associated risk, or not taking reasonable care that the product suits the buyer.

Front running: using non-public information to buy or sell securities, futures or options ahead of a substantial order in the same or related securities, expecting the price to move once the information is public. Typically a dealer or broker places his own or the firm's order ahead of a pending client order. It violates Section 12A (a), (b) and (e) of the SEBI Act, 1992, or Regulations 3(a) to (d) and 4(q) of PFUTP.

A dealer gets a client order to buy 5 lakh shares of ABC Ltd, enough to push the price up from ₹200. He first buys 10,000 shares for himself at ₹200, then executes the client order. The price rises to ₹206 and he sells, pocketing ₹60,000. That is front running.
blocks.title: Front running

items.title: Insider trading (PIT, 2015)
points: Trading on UPSI about the company (results, mergers, dividends...)
Insider = connected person or anyone with UPSI

items.title: Front running (PFUTP, 2003)
points: Trading ahead of a large pending order using knowledge of that order
Typically a dealer or broker jumping ahead of a client

items: Where SEBI has reasonable grounds to believe trading is detrimental to investors or the market, it can order an investigation of the intermediary or persons associated with the market.
Based on the investigating officer's report, SEBI can suspend or cancel registration; violators are liable to penalty; SEBI can also run parallel civil enforcement proceedings on the same facts.

blocks.text: 'Entering into a transaction without intention to perform it or to change ownership' is a fraudulent and unfair trade practice (PFUTP), not insider trading or money laundering.

Under SCRA, trading in shares between persons who are not members of a recognised exchange is illegal, and exchange members must be SEBI-registered stock brokers. Dabba trading is trading by unregistered persons outside the exchange: they use prices from the exchange, internet or TV, note deals in a separate book (physical or electronic), settle only price differences without delivery, and use cash rather than banks to avoid an audit trail.

items: Investors face credit risk: the operator may default or go bankrupt, and investors have no access to the exchange's complaint redressal or arbitration mechanism.
Cash dealings breed black money, a parallel economy, money laundering and crime; cause tax evasion; offer no settlement guarantee; and bypass regulation.

head: SCRA section
What it prohibits
rows: Contracts in securities other than between members of a recognised exchange in a notified area (notified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette)
All contracts except spot delivery contracts and those permitted under SCRA and exchange rules are illegal
Dealing in securities without a licence from SEBI
Derivatives are legal only if traded on a recognised exchange and settled on its clearing house
Organising, assisting or being a member of an unrecognised stock exchange

blocks.text: Section 23(1) SCRA: contravening sections 13, 16, 17 or 19 is punishable with imprisonment up to 10 years, or fine up to ₹25 crore, or both. Section 25: these are cognizable offences under the CrPC, 1973, so state police can investigate. Section 26: state authorities can lodge complaints. Dabba trading also attracts IPC sections 406 (criminal breach of trust), 420 (cheating) and 120-B (criminal conspiracy). The workbook prints "130-B"; that is a typo for 120-B.
Dabba = box. Everything stays inside the operator's box: no exchange, no clearing guarantee, no bank trail, no grievance desk.
Punishment: 10 years / ₹25 crore, not 5 years / ₹10 crore. Section 23(1) lists 13, 16, 17 and 19 (18A is violated but is not in that list).

SEBI (Custodian) Regulations, 1996: a custodian must register with SEBI; to get the certificate it needs a minimum net worth of ₹75 crore and must be 'fit and proper' under Schedule II of the Intermediaries Regulations, 2008.

items: Chapter III sets out obligations; custodians follow the code of conduct in the Third Schedule and must review, monitor and evaluate their controls.
Custodial business must be separate and segregated from other activities; its officers and employees may not do any other activity.
An agreement with each client covering when securities and money are accepted or released and how rights / entitlements are received.
A separate custody account for each client, in the client's name; one client's assets never mixed with another's.
Internal controls against manipulation of records (including audits), safekeeping against theft and natural hazards, and compliance with SEBI's Investor Charter.

blocks.text: SEBI {KYC Registration Agency} Regulations, 2011: KYC Registration Agencies (KRAs) remove the need for an investor to repeat KYC with every intermediary and give a uniform KYC process. All members must register with one or more SEBI-registered KRAs.

head: Who
Obligation
Timeline
rows: Client may open an account and transact as soon as KYC is complete
Upload initial KYC of new clients to the KRA system
Within 3 working days of completing KYC
Send a letter to the client confirming details of initial / updated KYC (keep proof of dispatch)
Comprehensive audit of systems by an independent auditor; report to its Board
Send Action Taken Report on that audit to SEBI
Upload verified KYC to the Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCRR)

items: Intermediary: forward missing documents promptly if the KRA flags them; upload existing clients' data in the uniform format without duplication; provide KYC information when needed; keep electronic KYC records (physical records not necessary); maintain internal controls on data security.

KRA: provide KYC information in data and image form; coordinate with other KRAs to prevent duplication and keep formats uniform; keep an audit trail of uploads, changes and downloads; flag PAN-exempt clients (e.g. residents of Sikkim, UN entities / multilateral agencies exempt from tax).

blocks.text: KYC clock: 3 - 2 - 7. Intermediary uploads in 3 working days, KRA writes to the client in 2 working days, KRA pushes to CKYCRR in 7 days.

items.title: Included as 'intermediary' (Intermediaries Regs, 2008)
points: Persons under sections 11(2)(b), (ba) and 12(1), (1A) of the SEBI Act
AMCs (under the Mutual Funds Regulations, 1996)
Clearing members
Foreign portfolio investors
Trading members of derivatives or currency derivatives segments

items.title: Excluded
points: Foreign venture capital investors
Mutual funds
Collective investment schemes
Venture capital funds

blocks.text: The Regulations cover registration of intermediaries, general obligations (investor grievance redressal, compliance officer, investment advice, code of conduct), inspection and disciplinary proceedings.

Chapter III B, Usage of Artificial Intelligence: any SEBI-regulated person using AI / ML tools, built in-house or bought from third parties, is solely responsible for (a) privacy, security and integrity of investor and stakeholder data, (b) the output it relies on, and (c) compliance with applicable laws, whatever the scale of use. Chapter III C deals with verification of past risk and return metrics.

SEBI (Depositories and Participants) Regulations, 2018: registration, ownership and governance of depositories and DPs; their rights and obligations; and procedures for pledge and hypothecation, listing of securities, surrender of securities etc.
A mutual fund is not an 'intermediary' under these Regulations, but its AMC is. Using a third-party AI tool does not shift responsibility away from the regulated entity.

sections.title: Code of Conduct for Stock Brokers (Annexure 1)

blocks.text: Three groups of duties: general conduct, duties to investors, and duties to other brokers.

head: General: a stock broker shall
rows: Maintain high standards of integrity, promptitude and fairness
Act with due skill, care and diligence
Not indulge in manipulative, fraudulent or deceptive transactions or schemes, or spread rumours to distort the market or for personal gain
Not create a false market, alone or in concert, or harm investors or the smooth functioning of the market
Not indulge in excessive speculative business beyond reasonable levels not commensurate with his financial soundness
Abide by the Act, rules and regulations of the Government, SEBI and the exchange

head: Duty towards the investor
rows: Execute orders at the best available market price; not refuse a small investor merely because of the small volume
Promptly inform the client of execution or non-execution; pay promptly for securities sold and deliver securities bought promptly
Issue a contract note without delay for all transactions, in the exchange's form
Keep clients' personal investment and other confidential information confidential; no improper use
Not encourage trades solely to generate brokerage; no false or misleading quotations or advice to induce business
Not knowingly deal for a client who has failed to meet commitments with another broker
Disclose whether acting as principal or agent; avoid conflicts of interest, disclose any that arise, and never put the client's interest below his own
Recommend only what he reasonably believes is suitable for the client, based on the client's holdings, finances and objectives

When giving investment advice in public media, disclose his interest (and that of dependent family members and employer), including long or short positions; an employee giving advice must make the same disclosure
Have adequately trained staff to give fair, prompt and competent service

head: Duty towards other stock brokers
rows: Cooperate in comparing unmatched transactions; not knowingly deliver bad delivery documents, and help replace them promptly
Cooperate to protect clients' rights to dividends, bonus shares, rights shares and other entitlements
Complete settlement obligations with other brokers
Not advertise his business publicly unless permitted by the exchange
Not use unfair means to poach clients from other brokers
Submit required returns to SEBI and the exchange, with no false or misleading statements

blocks.text: Count them: 6 - 10 - 6 (general, investor, other brokers). The investor list is longest because the client comes first.

A broker may not refuse a small investor because the volume is small, and may not advertise without exchange permission. Media advice requires disclosing the interest of dependent family members and the employer too.

flashcards.q: Four participants of the securities market?
flashcards.a: Investors, issuers, intermediaries and regulators

flashcards.q: Who is a Retail Individual Investor?
flashcards.a: An individual (resident, NRI or HUF) applying for not more than ₹2 lakh

flashcards.q: Who is a Non-Institutional Investor?
flashcards.a: Anyone other than RIIs and institutional investors, e.g. family offices, corporates, partnership firms

flashcards.q: Which Category II FPIs are treated as non-institutional?
flashcards.a: Corporate bodies, individuals and family offices

flashcards.q: Are pension funds and university funds Category I or II FPIs?
flashcards.a: Category I

flashcards.q: Individual accredited investor criteria?
flashcards.a: Income ₹2 cr+; or net worth ₹7.5 cr+ (half financial); or income ₹1 cr+ with net worth ₹5 cr+ (half financial)

flashcards.q: Who issues accreditation certificates?
flashcards.a: Accreditation Agencies: subsidiaries of depositories and stock exchanges, based only on KYC and financial information

flashcards.q: Accreditation validity?
flashcards.a: 2 years if criteria met for 1 preceding FY (or new entity); 3 years if met in each of 2 preceding FYs

flashcards.q: Main job of a market maker?
flashcards.a: Give continuous two-way quotes for a minimum amount with a reasonable bid-ask spread

flashcards.q: Where is market making mandatory?
flashcards.a: On the SME exchange, for all listed and traded scrips

flashcards.q: ADR vs GDR?
flashcards.a: ADR: issued by a US depository bank, trades in the US. GDR: non-US depository bank, mainly European exchanges.

flashcards.q: What is a Masala bond?
flashcards.a: A rupee-denominated bond issued outside India by an Indian entity

flashcards.q: First entity to issue an IDR in India?
flashcards.a: Standard Chartered Bank

flashcards.q: What are MIIs?
flashcards.a: Market Infrastructure Institutions: stock exchanges, clearing corporations and depositories

flashcards.q: What is novation?
flashcards.a: The clearing corporation becoming central counterparty, guaranteeing every trade on the exchange

flashcards.q: Pay-in vs pay-out?
flashcards.a: Pay-in: members bring funds / securities to the clearing corporation (first phase). Pay-out: clearing corporation delivers them (second phase).

flashcards.q: Who can become a Depository Participant?
flashcards.a: Banks, FIs, NBFCs, clearing corporations, RTAs, custodians, State Financial Corporations, SEBI-registered trading members

flashcards.q: Which member has clearing rights but no trading rights?
flashcards.a: Professional Clearing Member (and custodians)

flashcards.q: Trading-cum-self-clearing vs trading-cum-clearing member?
flashcards.a: Self-clearing clears only its own (and its clients') trades; trading-cum-clearing also clears other members' and custodial trades

flashcards.q: How many SEBI registrations does a broker on 3 exchanges need?
flashcards.a: One certificate of registration; each exchange / segment approval is still needed

flashcards.q: What is Base Minimum Capital?
flashcards.a: A deposit with the exchange against which no trading exposure is allowed, based on the member's risk profile

flashcards.q: Four fit and proper criteria?
flashcards.a: Integrity / reputation / character; no convictions or restraint orders; competence incl. solvency and net worth; not a wilful defaulter

flashcards.q: Is an Authorised Person a member of the exchange?
flashcards.a: No. An AP is the broker's agent; the broker is responsible for all its acts

flashcards.q: What if a custodian fails to confirm a trade?
flashcards.a: The trading member or its clearing member that executed the trade must settle it

flashcards.q: Who frames rules and who frames regulations under securities laws?
flashcards.a: Rules: Central Government. Regulations: SEBI. SEBI administers both.

flashcards.q: Under which section was SEBI established?
flashcards.a: Section 3 of the SEBI Act, 1992

flashcards.q: Where do appeals against SEBI orders go?
flashcards.a: Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT)

flashcards.q: Which Companies Act section delegates securities powers to SEBI?
flashcards.a: Section 24 (issue and transfer of securities, non-payment of dividend, for listed / to-be-listed companies)

flashcards.q: Two certificates a depository needs from SEBI?
flashcards.a: Certificate of registration and certificate of commencement of business

flashcards.q: PMLA punishment for money laundering?
flashcards.a: Rigorous imprisonment of 3 to 7 years plus fine; up to 10 years for scheduled narcotics offences

flashcards.q: Under PMLA, who bears the burden of proof?
flashcards.a: The accused must prove the proceeds are untainted (Section 24)

flashcards.q: Who is an insider under the PIT Regulations?
flashcards.a: A connected person, or anyone in possession of or with access to UPSI

flashcards.q: What is front running?
flashcards.a: Trading ahead of a substantial pending order using non-public knowledge of it, e.g. a dealer jumping a client order

flashcards.q: Punishment for dabba trading under SCRA Section 23(1)?
flashcards.a: Up to 10 years imprisonment, or fine up to ₹25 crore, or both

flashcards.q: Custodian minimum net worth?
flashcards.a: ₹75 crore

flashcards.q: KYC timelines for intermediary and KRA?
flashcards.a: Intermediary uploads in 3 working days; KRA writes to client in 2 working days; KRA uploads to CKYCRR in 7 days

flashcards.q: Is a mutual fund an 'intermediary' under the Intermediaries Regulations?
flashcards.a: No. Mutual funds, CIS, VCFs and FVCIs are excluded; AMCs are included.

questions.q: "Entering into a transaction in securities without the intention to perform it or to change ownership of the securities" is an example of:
options: A fraudulent and unfair trade practice
questions.why: It is listed in Regulation 4(2) of the PFUTP Regulations, 2003 as a manipulative, fraudulent or unfair trade practice.

questions.q: Which type of member does NOT have trading rights?
questions.why: A professional clearing member has only clearing rights; it clears trades of trading members and custodial participants.

questions.q: The clearing corporation providing a financial guarantee for all transactions executed on the exchange is known as:
questions.why: As central counterparty the clearing corporation guarantees every trade; this process is called novation.

questions.q: Under PMLA, records of transactions must be maintained for how long from the date of the transaction?
questions.why: Section 12 requires transaction records to be kept for five years from the date of the transaction.

questions.q: The Companies Act, 2013 delegates the power to regulate issue and transfer of securities of listed companies to:
questions.why: Section 24 makes SEBI the administrator of provisions on issue and transfer of securities and non-payment of dividend for listed / to-be-listed companies.

questions.q: A Retail Individual Investor is one who applies for specified securities for a value of not more than:
questions.why: An RII is an individual (resident, NRI or HUF) bidding for not more than ₹2 lakh; above that the individual is non-institutional.

questions.q: Under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019, pension funds and university funds fall under:
options: They are not eligible as FPIs
questions.why: Pension funds and university funds are listed among Category I FPIs.

questions.q: An applicant met the accredited investor criteria in each of the preceding two financial years. The accreditation certificate will be valid for:
questions.why: Criteria met in each of the preceding two FYs gives 3 years' validity; one FY (or a new entity) gives 2 years.

questions.q: Which of the following, on its own, qualifies an individual as an Accredited Investor?
options: Net worth of ₹2.5 crore in financial assets
questions.why: Income of ₹2 crore qualifies alone; ₹1 crore income qualifies only together with net worth of ₹5 crore (half in financial assets).

questions.q: Market making has been made mandatory for all scrips listed and traded on:
questions.why: For the SME exchange, market making is mandatory for all listed and traded scrips; elsewhere liquidity schemes are mainly run by exchanges.

questions.q: A Masala bond is:
options: A foreign currency bond issued in India by a foreign company
A rupee-denominated bond issued in India by a foreign bank
A foreign currency convertible bond issued by an Indian company
A rupee-denominated bond issued outside India by an Indian entity
questions.why: Masala bonds are rupee-denominated bonds issued outside India by Indian entities to raise rupee funds from foreign investors.

questions.q: Which of the following CANNOT become a Depository Participant as per SEBI regulations?
questions.why: DPs can be banks, FIs, NBFCs, clearing corporations, RTAs, custodians, State Financial Corporations and SEBI-registered trading members; an ordinary company is not on the list.

questions.q: What is the current minimum paid-up equity capital for a company seeking trading membership of a stock exchange?
questions.why: The eligibility table specifies minimum paid-up equity capital of ₹30 lakh (as specified from time to time).

questions.q: Who is responsible for all acts of omission and commission of an Authorised Person?
options: The trading member who appointed the AP
questions.why: The acts of the AP are deemed to be those of the trading member, which is responsible for them.

questions.q: A custodian to whom a trade is assigned fails to confirm it. Who must settle the trade?
options: The trading member or its clearing member who executed the trade
The clearing corporation's settlement guarantee fund
The client directly with the exchange
questions.why: If the custodian does not confirm, the onus of settling falls on the trading member or clearing member of the trading member who executed the trade.

questions.q: Under the securities laws, who frames the regulations and who frames the rules?
options: Regulations: RBI; Rules: Ministry of Corporate Affairs
questions.why: Rules under securities laws are framed by the Government and regulations by SEBI; all are administered by SEBI.

questions.q: The punishment for money laundering under Section 4 of PMLA (ordinary case) is rigorous imprisonment of:
questions.why: Section 4 prescribes rigorous imprisonment of not less than 3 years, extendable to 7 years, plus fine (10 years for certain scheduled offences).

questions.q: Under Section 24 of PMLA, when a person is charged with money laundering, the burden of proving that the proceeds are untainted lies on:
questions.why: The court presumes the proceeds are involved in money laundering unless the contrary is proved, so the burden is on the accused.

questions.q: A 'connected person' under the Insider Trading Regulations includes a person associated with the company at any time during how many months before the concerned act?
questions.why: A connected person is one who is or has been associated with the company during the six months prior to the concerned act.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT ordinarily treated as UPSI under the Insider Trading Regulations?
questions.why: Changes in ratings count as UPSI except ESG ratings; fund raising, auditor resignation and forensic audits are listed.

questions.q: Under Section 23(1) of SCRA, a person indulging in dabba trading in violation of sections 13, 16, 17 or 19 can be punished with:
options: Imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to ₹5 crore
Imprisonment up to 5 years or fine up to ₹10 crore
Imprisonment up to 10 years or fine up to ₹25 crore, or both
Only a monetary penalty imposed by the exchange
questions.why: Section 23(1) provides imprisonment up to ten years or fine up to ₹25 crore, or both; these offences are cognizable.

questions.q: After completing KYC of a new client, an intermediary must upload the KYC information to the KRA system within:
questions.why: The intermediary uploads within 3 working days; the KRA then writes to the client within 2 working days.

questions.q: Which of the following is excluded from the definition of 'intermediary' under the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008?
questions.why: The definition includes AMCs, clearing members and FPIs but excludes foreign venture capital investors, mutual funds, CIS and venture capital funds.

questions.q: A depository can directly open accounts and provide services to investors without going through a Depository Participant.
questions.why: A depository cannot open accounts directly; investors must enter into an agreement with it through a DP.

questions.q: Under the Code of Conduct, a stock broker shall not advertise his business publicly unless permitted by the stock exchange.
questions.why: This is one of the duties towards other stock brokers in Annexure 1.
